name: Breath mints

lead: Breath mints are mint-flavoured candies eaten to freshen breath. They are cheap and portable.
Sources describe the effect as short-term masking. Few clinical trials have tested mints specifically.

paras: Strong mint flavour covers odour, and sugar-free types may stimulate saliva.
Generally low risk; peppermint may worsen reflux and some mints contain sweeteners that bother sensitive people.

lead: Breath mints are small mint-flavoured candies eaten to improve breath odour before or after social occasions.[1] Wikipedia describes them as hard, soft or Scotch-style confections flavoured with mint or wintergreen oils.[1] Dental sources and Wikipedia's halitosis article characterise mints and similar products as short-term masking rather than treatment of the cause of odour.[2]

Published clinical work on mints is thin; one study compared oxidising lozenges with breath mints and chewing gum for malodour,[3] and another tested sorbitol-sweetened mints on salivary flow in people with dry mouth.[4]

paras: Hard mints include brands such as Altoids, Ice Breakers and Tic Tac; soft mints are butter or dinner mints; Scotch mints have a hard shell and softer centre.[1] Wikipedia notes that many mints citing natural mint contain little or none of it.[1]

Mints as a distinct product date to the 18th century, and their popularity grew in the early 20th century through urbanisation and advertising that stressed the social cost of bad breath.[1] In the United States a 2016 federal rule amended the label serving size for breath mints.[5]

Mints supply flavour and, in sugar-free versions, may stimulate saliva. Halitosis most often originates from bacterial biofilm on the tongue and gum disease, which mints do not address; Wikipedia describes mints as short-term masking.[2]

A 1997 study of 123 young adults compared oxidising lozenges with breath mints and chewing gum using judge-rated odour and volatile sulphide measures.[3] A 1989 study examined sorbitol-sweetened breath mints on salivary flow and plaque pH in people with dry mouth.[4] Most breath-odour trials in the literature test toothpastes and rinses rather than mints.[6][7]

Some mints contain sweeteners such as aspartame, and a 1988 report described intolerance reactions to aspartame in some individuals.[8] Peppermint may relax the lower oesophageal sphincter and aggravate reflux, according to Wikipedia.[1]
Mints are mentioned in appearance discussion as a quick, portable option for breath before social contact.

lore.intro: Mints are discussed as a convenience product, not a fix for chronic odour.

timeline.event: Mints appear as a distinct product.[1]
FDA final rule amends serving size for breath mints.[5]
